Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the AeroDef Technologies Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. As a reminder, the operator instructions are to press star one for questions. Please note this event is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Lisa Chen, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Lisa Chen:
Thank you, Operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to AeroDef Technologies' Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. Joining me today are David Thompson, Chief Executive Officer; Robert Kline, Chief Financial Officer; and Elena Vasquez, Chief Operating Officer.

Before we begin, I'd like to remind you that this call contains forward-looking statements within the meaning of the safe harbor provisions of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. Please refer to our SEC filings, including our most recent Form 10-K and 10-Q, for a complete discussion of risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially from these statements.

David Thompson:
Thank you, Lisa, and good morning, everyone. AeroDef Technologies delivered a solid performance in Q3, demonstrating the resilience of our business model and the strength of our diversified portfolio across commercial aerospace, defense systems, and space technologies. Our priorities remain focused on executing our strategy, driving operational excellence, and delivering value to our shareholders. Today, I'll highlight our overall company performance and key takeaways, the drivers behind our aftermarket strength like fleet utilization and maintenance cycles, and the geopolitical factors shaping defense spending. Robert will then walk through the financial details, including free cash flow.

Let me start with our overall company performance highlights and key takeaways. We're thrilled with how our diversified operations performed this quarter, showcasing the resilience and growth potential in this demanding industry. Q3 revenue reached $5.42 billion, up a strong 15% year-over-year and accelerating 20% from Q2. This topped our guidance by 3%, reflecting sharp execution in every segment. We're now raising full-year revenue guidance to $21.8 billion to $22.4 billion, pointing to 13-17% growth, propelled by surging defense needs and a commercial aviation recovery surpassing pre-pandemic benchmarks.

On profitability, adjusted EPS hit $2.12, a 30% jump year-over-year and $0.15 ahead of consensus. This came from adjusted EBITDA margins expanding 260 basis points to 19.1%, our best in years. We posted $520 million in operating cash flow, up 38% year-over-year, and $380 million in free cash flow, which supported $180 million in share repurchases and our 13th straight quarterly dividend hike to $0.52 per share. Book-to-bill was a healthy 1.28x, pushing total backlog to a record $48.2 billion—over four years of visibility at current rates.

By segment, Defense Systems, 53% of revenue, surged 22% to $2.87 billion. Standouts included a $3.1 billion IDIQ for Lot 6 of our advanced hypersonic boost-glide vehicles, similar to AGM-183A ARRW efforts, and full-rate production go-ahead for the MQ-100 Reaper successor in the Army's Future Tactical UAS program. Heightened tensions in the Indo-Pacific and Eastern Europe have ramped demand, with DoD hypersonics and CCA funding for NGAD-like initiatives at $4.8 billion in FY2024—up 42% year-over-year. International sales climbed 35%, capped by a $1.4 billion fixed-price pact with Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Defense for air defense integrations with Patriot-style AESA radar enhancements.

Commercial Aerospace, 27% of revenue, advanced 13% to $1.46 billion, boosted by ramps on Boeing 737 MAX and Airbus A320neo lines. Aerostructures and wing kits saw 20% forward pull from OEMs, with shipments up 28% to 1,650 sets. Supply chain pressures are fading—titanium forging lead times from Japan and U.S. alternatives to our prior VSMPO-AVISMA JV have dropped to 13 months from 21. We're set for 16% segment growth this fiscal year as widebody demand builds, with Boeing 777X entry-into-service in late 2025 releasing $950 million in held-back revenue.

Space & Mission Systems, our 20% revenue star, leaped 16% to $562 million, surpassing plans on Starshield-equivalent constellations and Artemis lunar hardware. We landed a $1.0 billion task order from the Space Development Agency's Tranche 2 for 52 pLEO satellites with hardened optical interlinks, echoing SpaceX Starlink but DoD-toughened for proliferated warfighter space. Asia-Pacific partnerships fueled 48% booking gains there.

Geographically, North America anchors us at 69% of revenue, with 92% on U.S. programs shielding us from currency swings. Europe added 17%, up 12% from F-35 support and Eurofighter enhancements amid Ukraine-spurred NATO hikes beyond 2% GDP. EMEA logistics costs rose 2-3% from Red Sea issues, but dual-sourcing via Indian and Turkish suppliers cushioned it. APAC at 14% is accelerating, with Australia offsets for Loyal Wingman drones under AUKUS Pillar II.

Key strategic moves are setting us up for ongoing superiority. Our $510 million R&D spend—4.7% of revenue—delivered wins like digital twin predictive maintenance swapping out F-35 ALIS, cutting downtime 32% and lifting aftermarket margins to 23.5%. We're pushing solid-state batteries for hybrid-electric in eVTOLs, aiming certification with Joby partners by 2026. Lean sigma and AI manufacturing optimization added 170 basis points to margins, with plants at 93% utilization. $250 million in reshoring for rare earths and composites has de-risked us.

In summary, defense tailwinds from great power rivalry lock in 96% backlog conversion through 2027. Commercial rebound is solid, with IATA eyeing 4.8 billion passengers this year. Our 1.2x net debt-to-EBITDA and top-tier supplier status minimize risks. Q4 revenue guides $5.6-$5.8 billion, full-year EPS $8.10-$8.40. We're raising expectations through scaled execution where innovation dominates.

Now, shifting to the drivers of our aftermarket performance, which was exceptional this quarter. Our Commercial Aviation Aftermarket grew 18% year-over-year to $1.85 billion, making up 43% of total revenue, while adjusted EBITDA margins widened 320 basis points to 33.1%. Defense Aftermarket rose 13% to $890 million, supported by ongoing platform use amid worldwide tensions. Let's unpack the main drivers: fleet utilization, maintenance cycles, and our forward-looking technical efforts.

Fleet utilization is the primary engine for aftermarket needs. Worldwide narrowbody utilization averaged 79% of pre-pandemic norms this quarter—rising from 73% in Q3 last year and 69% in Q2—backed by 15% year-over-year growth in global revenue passenger kilometers per IATA. For our key installed base of more than 12,500 engines on wing, including CFM LEAP-1A/1B and PW1100G on A320neo and A220 aircraft, single-aisle utilization reached 83%. Each extra flight hour spurs 15-20% more need for line-replaceable units such as ECS modules and thrust reversers.

By region, North America led with U.S. majors like Delta and United hitting 86% on 737 MAX and A321neo, driven by capacity expansions—Delta boosted narrowbody available seat miles by 5%. Europe trailed at 75%, hampered by Pratt & GTF PW1100G issues grounding 16-21% of A320neos at Lufthansa and easyJet, but we gained via Installed Fleet Management deals, adding $480 million in life-limited parts orders. Asia-Pacific varied, with Chinese COMAC C919 operators at 77% but supply-limited; our Shanghai MRO JV grew 27% quarter-over-quarter. Middle East carriers like Emirates and Qatar flew at 89%, their A380 and 777X ops lifting widebody spares 24%.

Maintenance cycles are speeding up in both commercial and defense, offering years of foresight. Commercial heavy checks increased 24% year-over-year, C-checks shortening to 17-23 months on A320/737 fleets from intense ops. LEAP engine shop visits rose to 1.25 per 10,000 cycles—over the 1.0 norm—due to higher HPT blade wear on inspections. This drove 30% MRO revenue growth to $1.18 billion, with Singapore and Phoenix shops at 96% occupancy.

In defense, F-35 readiness topped 67% from 59% last year per JSF SPO, boosting F135 services 18%, including overhauls and coatings. Red Sea routes and Ukraine losses compressed F-16 and Eurofighter cycles, increasing avionics demand.

Our technical pushes amplify these: Predictive Health Management on 72% of LEAPs uses AI digital twins for 93% shop visit accuracy, slashing unscheduled issues 37% for IndiGo-like clients. Additive manufacturing trimmed hot-section leads from 24 to 8 weeks, adding 16% pricing on nozzle fixes. With Lockheed on F-35 ALIS NextGen, PSP fill rates hit 98.5%.

We're emphasizing high-retention aftermarket via ESA contracts like TotalCare, now 57% of commercial base—up from 49%—yielding 41%+ margins vs. 26% spot. Defense backlog at $12.8 billion, 62% U.S./NATO-tied, dodges OEM pressures like at RTX or GE. Risks like GTF fixes post-2025 exist, but our mix—42% engines, 29% airframe, 29% defense—shields us. We expect 15-17% aftermarket growth in FY2025, utilization at 81%+, bays full to 2028, margins up 120-160 basis points with PHM expansion.

A critical backdrop here is the geopolitical factors influencing defense spending, which are fueling much of our momentum. These aren't fleeting; they're creating enduring demand, with funded backlog at $130 billion, up 15% year-over-year, and total remaining performance obligations over $188 billion. Global defense outlays hit $2.26 trillion last year per SIPRI, the ninth straight rise and fastest growth pace since the 1980s at 7% nominal. Peer rivals like Russia and China, hybrid risks, and supply disruptions are hastening buys. U.S. FY2024 NDAA at $890 billion—3.5% real growth—prioritizes hypersonics, CCA, and tough C4ISR; our A&D booked $4.5 billion in Q3, including $1.9 billion IDIQ for F-35 Lot 17 sustainment.

In Europe, Ukraine is the spark. Western aid exceeds $210 billion since 2022, with $63 billion U.S. supplementals pulling Javelin deliveries up 27%, Ukraine using 10,500+ units; Poland and Finland added $2.7 billion fire units. NATO's 2% pledge now covers 24 of 32 allies, spiking budgets 18% to €292 billion in 2024. Germany's €100 billion fund backs Eurofighter Tranche 4 and Patriot PAC-3, where we integrate. European backlog up 24% QoQ to $33 billion, including $6.5 billion AUKUS Pillar II for quantum comms and AI battle management. We're putting $480 million into FY2024 IR&D for DEWs against Russian drones, edging BAE.

Indo-Pacific sees China's gray-zone moves, spending $300 billion up 7.5%. U.S. Pacific Deterrence Initiative funds $9.5 billion for Virginia Block V subs and NGAD. Our LRASM reached full production, $1.2 billion Navy awards from Taiwan scenarios needing 2,200 sorties. Japan hits 2% GDP by 2027 with ¥45 trillion ($295 billion) plan, driving P-8A and MQ-4C sales; APAC backlog up 20% to $42 billion, plus $3.6 billion South Korea KF-21 Link-16. We're fast-tracking CCA under $1.7 billion Vanguard with AFRL for 2026 attritables vs. DF-17.

Middle East proxy fights boost AMD: Israel's systems hit 92% intercepts on 13,000+ threats since Oct 2023, Tamir up 37%. Abraham Accords unlock Saudi F-15EX $115 billion, UAE THAAD; $52 billion AMD market to 2030. CENTCOM adds $4.5 billion prepositioning, NASAMS in Qatar. MENA backlog $23 billion, up 13%, with offsets for ESSM Block 2 local builds.

Forward, DoD Replicator's $1.1 billion for 1,100+ autonomy by 2025 favors Ghost Bat wingmen and Anduril ties. Titanium up 42% from sanctions, but $2.3 billion composites integration hits 96% delivery. Risks: election sequestration (5-11% cuts post-2025 CBO), China rare earth curbs. Diversified contracts—56% fixed-price, 29% cost-plus—give 13.1% margins; FY2024 revenue $29.2-$29.8 billion, 12-13% EPS growth.

Geopolitics is our lasting boost: 9-11% A&D CAGR to 2030, us gaining 160 bps share via 5th-gen stealth, AI fusion, hypersonics.

We are particularly excited about the recent advancements in our NGAD program and its potential to transform air dominance and fuel future growth. We are seeing strong demand for our defense systems, and our commercial aerospace business is recovering steadily.

Robert Kline:
Thank you, David. Now, let's turn to the financials. In Q3, we reported revenue of $5.42 billion, representing a 15% increase year-over-year. Our earnings per share were $2.12. We continue to maintain a strong balance sheet with $5.4 billion in cash and equivalents. Our guidance for the full year has been raised as David noted. We are actively managing our costs and investing in key growth initiatives. We are also focused on returning capital to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases.

Our specific financial highlights include gross margin of 29.4%, operating income of $1.39 billion, and free cash flow of $1.65 billion.

Diving deeper into free cash flow generation and utilization, a pillar of our financial health in this volatile Aerospace & Defense space. FCF—operating cash minus CapEx—gauges our capacity to grow, reward owners, and weather supply inflation and labor crunches.

Headlines beat plans, affirming portfolio maturity. Q3 FCF was $1.65 billion, up 28% year-over-year, our 12th consecutive positive quarter. Year-to-date $3.25 billion, tracking full-year $6.2-$6.7 billion—18-23% above 2023's $5.3 billion.

Generation led by $2.35 billion operating cash, from $148 billion backlog up 9% sequentially. Aeronautics, via F-35 LRIP with Lockheed, gave 47%, cash conversion 107% of EBITDA on DoD/allied milestones. Missiles/Fire Control, 14.8% margins, contributed 32% from ARRW hypersonic deliveries amid Pacific strains.

Space Systems added $480 million from SpaceX/OneWeb sats, 32% YoY GaN payload ramp. Cash conversion 117% of net income, DSO down to 64 days from 71 via FAR-tied automation.

CapEx was $790 million, 3.4% of sales, in 3-4% range. Focused on: digital thread at Fort Worth/Huntsville with Siemens NX/PTC Windchill, trimming NGAD engineering 22%; AM scale for UH-60M titanium blades, cutting costs 37%; $170 million rare earth domestic processing post-Ukraine.

U.S. shone with DoD Ukraine/Indo-Pacific supplements lifting fixed-price 20%. Europe 24% of cash via F-35 NATO buys (Poland/Finland), backlog speeding on 2% GDP vows. APAC up 42% YoY from AUKUS hypersonics, P-8 sales Australia/Korea. Commercial 16% of flow, offset Boeing 737 MAX delays with $220 million inventory.

Utilization follows 50/30/20: 50% shareholders, 30% debt cut, 20% growth. Q3: $820 million to owners—$460 million dividends (1.9% yield, 11% hike), $360 million buybacks under $3.5 billion program, retiring 1.3% shares at $292 avg, ROIC >16% vs. Northrop/RTX.

Debt paydown $490 million, net debt 2.0x EBITDA from 2.4x start, on track for 1.9x end. Dry powder for M&A, $1.2 billion tagged for directed energy bolt-ons like L3Harris-CACI.

Growth 20% or $330 million: $170 million IRAD CCA drones Air Force, $160 million JADC2 with Palantir/Anduril for 550 bps margins by 2026 software warfare.

Risks: Boeing FAA holds slowing OEMs, shutdowns hitting Q4 pays. Tailwinds: FY25 NDAA $900 billion, Europe rearm. Guide 97-102% FCF/EBITDA, Q4 $1.7-$1.9 billion.

Our FCF powers us past peers like Boeing negatives, funding multi-domain ops.

Operator:
Thank you. We will now begin the question and answer session. As a reminder, press star one for questions. Our first question comes from Josh Friedman with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Josh Friedman:
Good morning, team. Can you provide more color on the drivers of aftermarket performance, especially fleet utilization regionally?

David Thompson:
Certainly, Josh. As I detailed earlier, global narrowbody utilization at 79% is a major tailwind, with North America at 86% from U.S. carriers' expansions, Europe catching up despite GTF challenges where we've secured LLP orders, and Middle East at 89% driving widebody spares. Maintenance cycles compressing and our PHM tech are layering on visibility through 2028.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Emily Carter with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Emily Carter:
Hi, thanks. I'm curious about free cash flow generation outlook and how you're utilizing it amid M&A interest?

Robert Kline:
Emily, great question. We're guiding strong YTD momentum to $6.2-$6.7 billion full-year, with Q4 robust on backlog pulls and DoD payments. Utilization sticks to 50/30/20—shareholders first via buybacks/dividends, then delever to under 2x, balance growth like CCA IRAD and tuck-in deals in energy weapons.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Mike Patel with Barclays. Please go ahead.

Mike Patel:
Thanks. Regarding the geopolitical factors, how are they flowing through to backlog stability?

David Thompson:
Mike, spot on. Ukraine aid, Indo-Pacific pivots, and Mideast AMD are structural, swelling funded backlog 15% to $130 billion. Europe up 24% QoQ on NATO rearm, APAC 20% from AUKUS/Japan, with Replicator autonomy adding urgency—95%+ conversion locked through 2027.

David Thompson:
Thank you for your questions. In closing, I'm confident in our ability to navigate the current environment and deliver long-term value to our shareholders. We remain focused on our strategic priorities, operational excellence, and innovation.

Lisa Chen:
Thank you for joining us today. This concludes our Q3 2024 earnings call. A replay and transcript will be available on our investor relations website.

Operator:
This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.
